**Lijia Zhang** (Chinese:张丽佳; pinyin:_Zhāng Lìjiā_; born May 12, 1964, in Nanjing) is a Chinese-born writer, journalist, social commentator and public speaker. Her work focuses on contemporary China, particularly social change, gender and women’s lives, economic transformation, inequality, shifting social values and China’s evolving role in the global order. She writes regularly in English for international publications.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-1)
Born in Nanjing, Zhang spent ten years working in a state-owned factory producing intercontinental missiles before becoming a journalist and writer. She is the author of the memoir “Socialism Is Great!”: A Worker’s Memoir of the New China and the novel Lotus, and co-author of the oral history China Remembers. Her journalism and commentary have appeared in publications including the South China Morning Post, The Guardian, Newsweek and The New York Times.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-2)
Zhang describes herself as a “cultural bridge” between China and the wider world—a role she regards as her self-appointed mission.
Lijia Zhang on Sky TV's discussion program with Francis Fukuyama in 2022

## Early life and education
[edit]
Zhang was born into a working-class family in Nanjing and grew up in severe poverty. In 1980, when she was sixteen, her family took her out of school so that she could earn money. She began working at a military factory producing intercontinental missiles. During her decade there, she found solace in literature and taught herself English, initially as an escape from the routine of factory life.
During the 1989 protest movement, Zhang organised workers at her factory in support of the student-led demonstrations. She later wrote about her experience of the movement for The New York Times.
Zhang went to Britain in 1990, where she studied journalism. She later returned to China and began working with foreign correspondents before establishing herself as a journalist and writer. In 2003, she studied creative writing at Goldsmiths, University of London, receiving an MA.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-3)

## Journalism and Career
[edit]
After returning to China in the early 1990s, Zhang began her journalism career by assisting foreign correspondents as a researcher, interpreter and fixer. She subsequently wrote for international newspapers and magazines, with her work examining China’s social, cultural and economic transformation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-4)
Her articles and commentary have appeared in publications including the South China Morning Post, The Guardian, The Financial Times, Newsweek, The New York Times, The Independent, The Japan Times and the Far Eastern Economic Review. Her work explores inequality, shifting social values and China’s evolving role in the global order.
Zhang is also a commentator on China for international broadcast media. She has appeared on the BBC, Channel 4, CNN, NPR, ABC Australia and Al Jazeera. (Impact Podcast) In 2008, she was the subject of the BBC television documentary [Peschardt’s People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peschardt's_People "Peschardt's People"). In 2026, she was interviewed at length for the Impact Podcast about China’s social transformation and its relationship with the wider world.
Zhang co-authored China Remembers (Oxford University Press, 1999), an oral history of the People’s Republic of China.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-5)
Her memoir, “Socialism Is Great!”: A Worker’s Memoir of the New China, recounts her decade working in a missile factory during China’s reform era and her transition from factory worker to writer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-6) The hardback edition was published in the United States by Atlas & Co. in 2008, followed by a paperback edition from Random House a year later.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-7) The memoir has also been published in Australia, India, the Netherlands, Italy, France, Brazil, Poland, South Korea and Germany. Historian Jonathan Spence called it “a truly original contribution to our understanding of modern China”.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-8)

## Journalism and Career
Her first novel, Lotus, was published by Macmillan in 2017. Set in Shenzhen, it follows a young migrant woman who becomes a sex worker. The novel was inspired by Zhang’s discovery of a family secret: her grandmother had been sold to a brothel as a young woman.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-9) The novel explores migration, sexuality, gender and the tension between traditional expectations and individual aspirations in contemporary China. It was named one of NPR’s notable books of 2017[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-10) and was later discussed by Zhang on the BBC World Service’s World Book Club.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-11)
Zhang also writes short fiction. Her story “Permission” appeared in Silkroad magazine’s Short Story Anthology in 2017, while “Bright and Fragrant” was included in The Best Asian Speculative Fiction 2018.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-13)
She is currently completing a historical novel based on the life of Qiu Jin, a revolutionary and pioneering Chinese feminist who defied the social conventions of her time by unbinding her feet, wearing men’s clothing and organising an armed uprising against Qing rule.
Zhang writes primarily in English despite being a native Chinese speaker. She has said that the decision followed an unsuccessful attempt in the early 1990s to publish a Chinese-language book about Western perceptions of Mao Zedong. According to Zhang, the manuscript was rejected by Chinese censors for being considered “too negative”, after which she decided to write in English.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-14)
She has described writing in English as a form of liberation, both politically and creatively, while also acknowledging the linguistic and cultural losses involved in writing in a second language.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-15)

Lijia, talk a little bit about what does this mean? Where did you grow up in China and how did you get on this ever fascinating journey that you’re on where you really were a rocket factory girl, which I want you to explain who then turned, of course, prolific writer.
Lijia: I was born into a poor working class family in Nanjing, in Eastern part of China on the banks of Yangtze River. I grew up in the residential compound which belonged to the factory my mother worked for. All my neighbors worked for the same factory, and all my friends were the children of the factory workers. But I had a grand plan. I wanted to go to university, I wanted to become a writer and journalist.
John: But what informed you at such a young and tender age to actually have a big dream? Because usually when children are shown a lot of options, they don’t know how to dream big. Where did you get the opportunity to have a big dream like that?

Lijia: I guess I was a good student. In China to be a good student you needed to have a good memory. So I just remembered I had a good memory. That’s all you need to be a good student. Totally before that China resumed the system before that during the cultural revolution and university was stopped. I was a good student. My teacher encouraged me to pursue dream. Particularly also I had a dream to become a writer and journalist. Actually I didn’t quite understand the difference between writing and journalist. But anyway, I want to go to university become a writer. The teacher often at school, my teachers often read my writing as a good example to show other students. I won competition in writing which was why I wanted to be a writer and journalist. But when I was 16, I was taken outta school. I was 16, that was 1980. So you clever people can quickly work out how old I’m precisely. That’s all [inaudible].
John: You’re younger than me, so that’s all that matters at this point.
Lijia: Only slightly, John.
John: You were 16 and pulled out by the government to go to work?
Lijia: No. My parents and basically my mother. Because at that time there was a temporary policy which allowed children to take over their parents’ job if parents retired early. That was way to solve the soaring unemployment at that time. So my mother being educated and she never saw the benefit of education. She thought that the most important thing for mother was to secure a job, especially a prestigious job. Like my mother had she worked for the state-owned enterprise. Among other products the factory produced intercontinental missiles that were capable of reaching North America. I have to say though, sorry, I have to stress. I was a no nuclear scientist. I did the most basic job, the framework go back. So I didn’t know any top nuclear secrets. Sorry.
John: How long were you a rocket factory girl? You were there started when you were 16. How long did that go for?
Lijia: I worked there for 10 years.
John: Did you still nurture your dream of becoming a writer and potentially also a reporter or columnist as well?

Lijia: Well, I think at that time I had these grand dreams and then I found myself being tractor at the bottom of the factory well become a factory worker. The factory was interesting in some way. It is like it was a mini communist state. So it provided lots of things for workers, like the flat we had were allocated by the factory. There was the factory provided the medical care, the factory provided dining hall. So we all provided lots of things but there were lots of control. The first day we entered the factory we were given a long list of things not to do. No lipsticks, no skinny jeans, no trousers with flares either, no dating with three years of entering the factory. So there were just lots of rules and I just wanted to as escape route, so I decided to teach myself English. So of course, looking back and learning English has effectively changed my life.
John: Wait a second. This is when you were 16.
Lijia: I began to teach my self English halfway through the factory.
John: You were 21.
Lijia: Yes. 42 years I think.
John: [crosstalk] It’s about 1985 there was no internet, there was none of these easy courses that now have become [inaudible] in our life. How did you go about what sounds like a very difficult task of teaching yourself English? What was available to you? What tools were available to you?
Lijia: Of course, as you pointed out today there are so many courses on offer. There’s so many devices. You could watch Pirate the latest Hollywood movies, but none of those things when I was young. I had to borrow a radio from my cousin. Even even radio was a luxury. We didn’t have a television. I forgot to mention how poor we were. And why my parents took me out of the school because we were so poor.
Like then every month we were only allowed a tiny amount meat. Back then everything like cooking oil, meat, milk. All these things were Russian rice. To satisfy our craving for meat my brother and I used to go out to catch Cicadas and then roast them over small bonfire and munch them up. Have you tried it?

# Lijia Zhang
Lijia Zhang is a factory-worker-turned writer, columnist, social commentator, and public speaker. She was born into a poor worker’s family in Nanjing, on the banks of Yangtze River. At 16, she was taken out of school and put to work at a missile factory, where she taught herself English. Her articles have appeared in many international publications, including _South China Morning Post_, _The Guardian_, _Newsweek_, and The New York Times. She is the co-author of _China Remembers_, an oral history of the People’s Republic of China. Her memoir, _Socialism Is Great!_, about her decade-long experience working at the factory in the 1980’s, was first published in the U.S. in 2008 and has been translated into numerous languages around the world. She is a regular speaker on the BBC, Channel 4, CNN, and National Public Radio. She was a recipient of the prestigious fellowship for the International Writers’ Program at the University of Iowa in 2009. She divides her time between England and China.

# Lijia Zhang
Lijia Zhang is a factory-worker-turned writer, columnist, social commentator, and public speaker. She was born into a poor worker’s family in Nanjing, on the banks of Yangtze River. At 16, she was taken out of school and put to work at a missile factory, where she taught herself English. Her articles have appeared in many international publications, including _South China Morning Post_, _The Guardian_, _Newsweek_, and The New York Times. She is the co-author of _China Remembers_, an oral history of the People’s Republic of China. Her memoir, _Socialism Is Great!_, about her decade-long experience working at the factory in the 1980’s, was first published in the U.S. in 2008 and has been translated into numerous languages around the world. She is a regular speaker on the BBC, Channel 4, CNN, and National Public Radio. She was a recipient of the prestigious fellowship for the International Writers’ Program at the University of Iowa in 2009. She divides her time between England and China.

**Lijia Zhang** (Chinese:张丽佳; pinyin:_Zhāng Lìjiā_; born May 12, 1964, in Nanjing) is a Chinese-born writer, journalist, social commentator and public speaker. Her work focuses on contemporary China, particularly social change, gender and women’s lives, economic transformation, inequality, shifting social values and China’s evolving role in the global order. She writes regularly in English for international publications.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-1)
Born in Nanjing, Zhang spent ten years working in a state-owned factory producing intercontinental missiles before becoming a journalist and writer. She is the author of the memoir “Socialism Is Great!”: A Worker’s Memoir of the New China and the novel Lotus, and co-author of the oral history China Remembers. Her journalism and commentary have appeared in publications including the South China Morning Post, The Guardian, Newsweek and The New York Times.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-2)
Zhang describes herself as a “cultural bridge” between China and the wider world—a role she regards as her self-appointed mission.
Lijia Zhang on Sky TV's discussion program with Francis Fukuyama in 2022

## Early life and education
[edit]
Zhang was born into a working-class family in Nanjing and grew up in severe poverty. In 1980, when she was sixteen, her family took her out of school so that she could earn money. She began working at a military factory producing intercontinental missiles. During her decade there, she found solace in literature and taught herself English, initially as an escape from the routine of factory life.
During the 1989 protest movement, Zhang organised workers at her factory in support of the student-led demonstrations. She later wrote about her experience of the movement for The New York Times.
Zhang went to Britain in 1990, where she studied journalism. She later returned to China and began working with foreign correspondents before establishing herself as a journalist and writer. In 2003, she studied creative writing at Goldsmiths, University of London, receiving an MA.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-3)
texts.2:
## Journalism and Career
[edit]
After returning to China in the early 1990s, Zhang began her journalism career by assisting foreign correspondents as a researcher, interpreter and fixer. She subsequently wrote for international newspapers and magazines, with her work examining China’s social, cultural and economic transformation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-4)
Her articles and commentary have appeared in publications including the South China Morning Post, The Guardian, The Financial Times, Newsweek, The New York Times, The Independent, The Japan Times and the Far Eastern Economic Review. Her work explores inequality, shifting social values and China’s evolving role in the global order.
Zhang is also a commentator on China for international broadcast media. She has appeared on the BBC, Channel 4, CNN, NPR, ABC Australia and Al Jazeera. (Impact Podcast) In 2008, she was the subject of the BBC television documentary [Peschardt’s People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peschardt's_People "Peschardt's People"). In 2026, she was interviewed at length for the Impact Podcast about China’s social transformation and its relationship with the wider world.
Zhang co-authored China Remembers (Oxford University Press, 1999), an oral history of the People’s Republic of China.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-5)
Her memoir, “Socialism Is Great!”: A Worker’s Memoir of the New China, recounts her decade working in a missile factory during China’s reform era and her transition from factory worker to writer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-6) The hardback edition was published in the United States by Atlas & Co. in 2008, followed by a paperback edition from Random House a year later.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-7) The memoir has also been published in Australia, India, the Netherlands, Italy, France, Brazil, Poland, South Korea and Germany. Historian Jonathan Spence called it “a truly original contribution to our understanding of modern China”.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-8)
texts.3:
## Journalism and Career
Her first novel, Lotus, was published by Macmillan in 2017. Set in Shenzhen, it follows a young migrant woman who becomes a sex worker. The novel was inspired by Zhang’s discovery of a family secret: her grandmother had been sold to a brothel as a young woman.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-9) The novel explores migration, sexuality, gender and the tension between traditional expectations and individual aspirations in contemporary China. It was named one of NPR’s notable books of 2017[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-10) and was later discussed by Zhang on the BBC World Service’s World Book Club.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-11)
Zhang also writes short fiction. Her story “Permission” appeared in Silkroad magazine’s Short Story Anthology in 2017, while “Bright and Fragrant” was included in The Best Asian Speculative Fiction 2018.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-13)
She is currently completing a historical novel based on the life of Qiu Jin, a revolutionary and pioneering Chinese feminist who defied the social conventions of her time by unbinding her feet, wearing men’s clothing and organising an armed uprising against Qing rule.
Zhang writes primarily in English despite being a native Chinese speaker. She has said that the decision followed an unsuccessful attempt in the early 1990s to publish a Chinese-language book about Western perceptions of Mao Zedong. According to Zhang, the manuscript was rejected by Chinese censors for being considered “too negative”, after which she decided to write in English.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-14)
She has described writing in English as a form of liberation, both politically and creatively, while also acknowledging the linguistic and cultural losses involved in writing in a second language.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-15)

John: Well, I think they put a lot of pressure on you right from the get go. But I think you’ve lived up to it as well. That’s a hotcake[?]. Where did you grow up in China and how did you get on this ever fascinating journey that you’re on where you really were a rocket factory girl, which I want you to explain who then turned, of course, prolific writer.
Lijia: I was born into a poor working class family in Nanjing, in Eastern part of China on the banks of Yangtze River. I grew up in the residential compound which belonged to the factory my mother worked for. All my neighbors worked for the same factory, and all my friends were the children of the factory workers. But I had a grand plan. I wanted to go to university, I wanted to become a writer and journalist.
John: But what informed you at such a young and tender age to actually have a big dream? Because usually when children are shown a lot of options, they don’t know how to dream big. Where did you get the opportunity to have a big dream like that?
texts.2:
Lijia: I guess I was a good student. In China to be a good student you needed to have a good memory. So I just remembered I had a good memory. That’s all you need to be a good student. Totally before that China resumed the system before that during the cultural revolution and university was stopped. I was a good student. My teacher encouraged me to pursue dream. Particularly also I had a dream to become a writer and journalist. Actually I didn’t quite understand the difference between writing and journalist. But anyway, I want to go to university become a writer. The teacher often at school, my teachers often read my writing as a good example to show other students. I won competition in writing which was why I wanted to be a writer and journalist. But when I was 16, I was taken outta school. I was 16, that was 1980. So you clever people can quickly work out how old I’m precisely. That’s all [inaudible].
John: You’re younger than me, so that’s all that matters at this point.
Lijia: Only slightly, John.
John: You were 16 and pulled out by the government to go to work?
Lijia: No. My parents and basically my mother. Because at that time there was a temporary policy which allowed children to take over their parents’ job if parents retired early. That was way to solve the soaring unemployment at that time. So my mother being educated and she never saw the benefit of education. She thought that the most important thing for mother was to secure a job, especially a prestigious job. Like my mother had she worked for the state-owned enterprise. Among other products the factory produced intercontinental missiles that were capable of reaching North America. I have to say though, sorry, I have to stress. I was a no nuclear scientist. I did the most basic job, the framework go back. So I didn’t know any top nuclear secrets. Sorry.
John: How long were you a rocket factory girl? You were there started when you were 16. How long did that go for?
Lijia: I worked there for 10 years.
John: Did you still nurture your dream of becoming a writer and potentially also a reporter or columnist as well?

It is like it was a mini communist state. So it provided lots of things for workers, like the flat we had were allocated by the factory. There was the factory provided the medical care, the factory provided dining hall. So we all provided lots of things but there were lots of control. The first day we entered the factory we were given a long list of things not to do. No lipsticks, no skinny jeans, no trousers with flares either, no dating with three years of entering the factory. So there were just lots of rules and I just wanted to as escape route, so I decided to teach myself English. So of course, looking back and learning English has effectively changed my life.
John: Wait a second. This is when you were 16.
Lijia: I began to teach my self English halfway through the factory.
John: You were 21.
Lijia: Yes. 42 years I think.
John: [crosstalk] It’s about 1985 there was no internet, there was none of these easy courses that now have become [inaudible] in our life. How did you go about what sounds like a very difficult task of teaching yourself English? What was available to you? What tools were available to you?
Lijia: Of course, as you pointed out today there are so many courses on offer. There’s so many devices. You could watch Pirate the latest Hollywood movies, but none of those things when I was young. I had to borrow a radio from my cousin. Even even radio was a luxury. We didn’t have a television. I forgot to mention how poor we were. And why my parents took me out of the school because we were so poor.
Like then every month we were only allowed a tiny amount meat. Back then everything like cooking oil, meat, milk. All these things were Russian rice. To satisfy our craving for meat my brother and I used to go out to catch Cicadas and then roast them over small bonfire and munch them up. Have you tried it?

## Early life and education
[edit]
Zhang was born into a working-class family in Nanjing and grew up in severe poverty. In 1980, when she was sixteen, her family took her out of school so that she could earn money. She began working at a military factory producing intercontinental missiles. During her decade there, she found solace in literature and taught herself English, initially as an escape from the routine of factory life.
During the 1989 protest movement, Zhang organised workers at her factory in support of the student-led demonstrations. She later wrote about her experience of the movement for The New York Times.
Zhang went to Britain in 1990, where she studied journalism. She later returned to China and began working with foreign correspondents before establishing herself as a journalist and writer. In 2003, she studied creative writing at Goldsmiths, University of London, receiving an MA.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-3)

## Journalism and Career
[edit]
After returning to China in the early 1990s, Zhang began her journalism career by assisting foreign correspondents as a researcher, interpreter and fixer. She subsequently wrote for international newspapers and magazines, with her work examining China’s social, cultural and economic transformation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-4)
Her articles and commentary have appeared in publications including the South China Morning Post, The Guardian, The Financial Times, Newsweek, The New York Times, The Independent, The Japan Times and the Far Eastern Economic Review. Her work explores inequality, shifting social values and China’s evolving role in the global order.
Zhang is also a commentator on China for international broadcast media. She has appeared on the BBC, Channel 4, CNN, NPR, ABC Australia and Al Jazeera. Historian Jonathan Spence called it “a truly original contribution to our understanding of modern China”.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-8)

## Journalism and Career
Her first novel, Lotus, was published by Macmillan in 2017. Set in Shenzhen, it follows a young migrant woman who becomes a sex worker.
